literal: A clansman, Nuzhen, led his division in submission.
idiomatic: Nuzhen, a kinsman of the line, brought his following in to submit.

literal: Nuzhen's elder brother Jian had earlier dwelt with the Helan tribe.
idiomatic: His elder brother Jian had long lived among the Helan.

literal: At this time Nuzhen asked to summon Jian and yield the division to him.
idiomatic: Now Nuzhen asked to call Jian in and turn the tribe over to him.

literal: Taizu, moved by the righteousness of it, granted his request.
idiomatic: Taizu, approving the act, allowed it.

literal: Once Jian held the division, deeming himself long indebted to He Ne for shelter, he sent his younger brother Qujin to present him with a golden horse.
idiomatic: When Jian took command, he felt himself long beholden to He Ne and sent his brother Qujin with a gift of a golden horse.

literal: He Ne's younger brother Ran'gan then said to him: "I have treated you brothers generously; now that you lead a division, you ought to come follow me."
idiomatic: He Ne's brother Ran'gan told him, "I have been generous to you two; now that you lead a division, you should come over to my side."

literal: Qujin asked Nuzhen about it.
idiomatic: Qujin put the matter to Nuzhen.

literal: Nuzhen said: "Our father was a subject attached to the state; for generations we have served with loyal fidelity.
idiomatic: Nuzhen replied, "Our father was the state's man; our house has served with loyalty for generations.

literal: I sought to preserve our name and honor intact, and for that reason I yielded the division.
idiomatic: I meant to keep our name whole, and that is why I yielded the tribe.

literal: Now you behave disgracefully and would betray your lord with divided hearts."
idiomatic: Now you act shamefully and would turn traitor with a double heart."

literal: He then killed Jian and Qujin.
idiomatic: He killed Jian and Qujin on the spot.

literal: When Ran'gan heard that he had killed his elder brother, he led horsemen to attack him; Nuzhen in fear moved his division to flee to Taizu.
idiomatic: Ran'gan, hearing his brother had been killed, led cavalry against him; Nuzhen in alarm moved his people to seek refuge with Taizu.

literal: Taizu went out in person to welcome him and sent envoys to reprimand Ran'gan and halt him.
idiomatic: Taizu rode out to meet him and sent envoys to rebuke Ran'gan and make him stop.

literal: Grateful, Nuzhen offered his younger sister for the inner palace; Taizu took her.
idiomatic: Nuzhen, moved by the grace shown him, offered his younger sister to the inner palace, and Taizu took her.

literal: Later Taizu campaigned against Xian at Mayi, pursued him to Mize, and routed him utterly.
idiomatic: Later Taizu attacked Liu Xian at Mayi, chased him to Mize, and broke him completely.

literal: Wei Chen maintained friendly relations with Murong Chui and sent him three thousand horses; Chui dispatched Murong Liang to receive them.
idiomatic: Wei Chen was on good terms with Murong Chui and sent him three thousand horses; Chui sent Murong Liang to meet the herd.

literal: Xian defeated Liang's army and seized the horses.
idiomatic: Liu Xian smashed Liang's force and drove off the horses.

literal: Chui in anger sent his son Lin and his brother's son Kai against him; Xian fled to the western hills of Mayi.
idiomatic: Chui in fury sent his son Lin and his brother's son Kai to punish him; Xian fled into the western hills of Mayi.

literal: Lin with light cavalry pursued him, and he fled at last to Murong Yong at Changzi.
idiomatic: Lin pressed him with light horse until he took refuge with Murong Yong at Changzi.

literal: All his followers surrendered to Lin, and Lin resettled them at Zhongshan.
idiomatic: His whole following submitted to Lin, and Lin moved them to Zhongshan.

literal: Xian's younger brother Kang'ai: the account is in the Empresses' biography.
idiomatic: Liu Xian's brother Kang'ai is treated in the Empresses' biography.

literal: The historiographer says: In the age of the Founding Ancestor and of the Huan and Mu emperors, the royal enterprise had only just been laid, and exemplary virtue was not yet fully displayed.
idiomatic: The historiographer writes: Under the Founding Ancestor and Emperors Huan and Mu, the royal work had barely begun and moral influence had not yet spread.

literal: Cao and Han betook themselves to the season of galloping campaigns and made their own ground of merit and fame, [4] — men who may be called of purposeful mind and vision.
idiomatic: Cao and Han threw themselves into the hurrying age of war and carved out a place of merit and renown, [4] — true men of purpose and sight.

literal: The brothers Liu Kuren held loyalty as their heart; in fortune or decline they did not waver; the pure integrity they preserved showed purpose reaching far — yet both met untimely ends. A pity!
idiomatic: The Liu Kuren brothers took loyalty for their heart and did not shift between rise and fall; the pure constancy they kept looked far ahead — yet both died before their time. What a loss!

literal: Collation notes
idiomatic: Textual notes

literal: Cao erected a stele south of Dahang city. Qian's Textual Notes, juan 38, state: "This biography records the stele Wei Cao erected" (the transmitted citation here abbreviates the middle) "Alas, the court historiographers altered it and its original truth was lost."
idiomatic: Wei Cao set up a stele south of Dahang city. In Qian's Textual Notes, juan 38, we read that this chapter preserves his inscription in full, yet the historiographers mangled the record and the authentic text was lost.

literal: At the head of the inscription it reads: 'Scion of the Yellow Emperor of Wei.'
idiomatic: The opening line runs, 'Scion of the Yellow Emperor of Wei.'

literal: On examination, at that time there was as yet no title of Wei; judged by the sense of the text it ought to read 'of the Xianbei Tuoba clan.'
idiomatic: At that date there was no Wei designation yet; by sense it should read 'of the Xianbei Tuoba clan.'

literal: The stele was erected for Yiyi; it must have recorded the offices and ranks granted by Jin and the names of Yiyi and Yilu, yet the text calls them 'the two emperors Huan and Mu' — again an alteration by the historiographers."
idiomatic: The stone was raised for Yiyi and must have named the Jin-bestowed offices and both Yiyi and Yilu; calling them 'the two emperors Huan and Mu' is another historiographer's change."

literal: "In outward campaigns, he also repelled": in Northern History juan 20, this biography reads dong (campaign) as xun (merit).
idiomatic: "Outward campaigns also repelled": Northern History juan 20, this life, has dong (campaign) for xun (merit).

literal: Commentary: "In outward merit he also repelled" means he had the achievement of repelling external calamity; the inscription's closing line "merit that repelled the great scourge" bears the same sense.
idiomatic: Note: "outward merit also repelled" means merit in repelling foreign trouble; the stele's closing "merit that repelled the great scourge" is the same idea.

literal: It seems xun (merit) is correct.
idiomatic: Xun (merit) appears to be right.

literal: "The great chief Jiefo of the Bai tribe rebelled": in various editions bai (white/Bai) is written as yue (say).
idiomatic: "The Bai tribe's great chief Jiefo rebelled": editions read bai (Bai) as yue (say).

literal: Cefu juan 352
idiomatic: Cefu, juan 352

literal: 〈page 4180〉
idiomatic: folio 4180

literal: reads "bai" (White/Bai).
idiomatic: has "Bai."

literal: Commentary: Juan 1, Annalistic Preface, year 39 of Liwei states: "In the fourth month of summer they sacrificed to Heaven; the chieftains of all divisions came to assist in the rites — only the great chief of the Bai tribe stood apart and did not come.
idiomatic: Note: Annalistic Preface, juan 1, Liwei year 39: "Fourth month, summer sacrifice to Heaven; every division's chief came to assist — only the Bai tribe's great chief held back and did not attend.

literal: Again, year 3 of Yilu states "the great chief of the Bai tribe rebelled and entered Xihe."
idiomatic: Yilu year 3 also says "the Bai tribe's great chief rebelled and entered Xihe."

literal: The character yue is erroneous; the text is now emended according to Cefu.
idiomatic: Yue is a corruption; emended per Cefu.

literal: "Made their own ground of merit and fame": various editions lack the character ming (fame/name).
idiomatic: "Carved out a place of merit and renown": editions omit ming (fame).

literal: Palace Edition textual notes state: "Below gong (merit) Northern History
idiomatic: Palace Edition textual notes: "After gong (merit), Northern History

literal: 〈juan 20〉
idiomatic: (juan 20)

literal: has the character ming; that reading should be accepted.
idiomatic: has ming; that text should stand.

literal: Commentary: "merit and fame" balances with "galloping" above; here the character ming has dropped out; supplied now according to Northern History.
idiomatic: Note: "merit and fame" pairs with "hurrying" above; the word ming dropped here and is restored from the Northern History.
